polygon-angles.why: Any polygon with ~n~ sides splits into ~n - 2~ triangles from one vertex, so its interior angles total ~(n - 2) \times 180~ degrees. The exterior angles, one at each vertex, always total 360 degrees however many sides there are, because walking round the shape turns you through one full circle.
traps: Dividing the total by ~n~ only gives each angle for a *regular* polygon. An irregular one shares the same total unevenly.
The exterior route is usually quicker: each exterior angle of a regular polygon is ~\f{360}{n}~.

quadrilateral-properties.why: The quadrilaterals form a family tree, not a list. A square is a rectangle and a rhombus; rectangles, rhombuses and parallelograms are all parallelograms. Knowing the hierarchy tells you at once which properties a shape inherits.
traps: Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square. The arrows in the hierarchy only point one way.
A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides in the definition used here. Some books say *at least* one, so check which your course uses.

quadrilateral-proofs.why: To prove a shape is a particular quadrilateral, you need a *sufficient* set of facts, not all of them. Both pairs of opposite sides equal makes a parallelogram. Add a right angle and it is a rectangle; add equal adjacent sides and it is a rhombus.
traps: Claim only what the evidence supports. A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle, not necessarily a square.
